lawyer: Mr. S.K. Sinha with Mr. Md. Shafiqur Rahman, Advocate ------ For the petitioner.
parties:
Al-Helal Rice Mills Ltd ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangsta ------Respondent
full_judgment:
A M Mahmudur Rahman J: The petitioner is a private Ltd. company. In 1978 the Department of Food proposed to the Managing Director of the company whether the company is desirous of obtaining loan to establish an automatic rice mill for milling of paddy to be supplied by the said Department and in case it so desire they would make necessary arrangements for the fund from Asian Development Bank. The petitioner applied for such fund. Being satisfied with the application on Inquiry it accepted the scheme of the petitioner for obtaining such loan and the respondent Sangstha sanctioned initially loan for U.S.$ 1,33,000/- for supply of the machinery for the petitioner M/s. Al-Helal Automatic Rice Mill Ltd. and the Sangstha selected Indian suppliers and the money sanctioned was in yen at 2,91,83,486 equivalent to Indian Currency Rs. 9,80,000/-Machinery and equipment were sent to Bangladesh and the petitioner released the same. Supplied machinery fell short of the required one, petitioner repeatedly made claim to the B.S.R.S for direction to the supplier to replace the wanting parts of the machinery. Further the quality of the machinery, were defective and inferior one and was in terms of tender. Inspite of the repeated demand of the petitioner to the respondent to make book loss for its failure. The petitioner had to renovate the same at his own cost. The result was the mill could not be run in a full swing and ultimately had to stop its functioning for such defective machineries. In such a situation the respondent Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Snagsta made demand to repay the loan with interest. The petitioner replied that for no fault of it mill could not be run and it did not violate any terms of loan agreement. The petitioner further prayed for exemption of interest and the privilege of installment for payment of the loan. However, the petitioner paid Tk. 8,88,255/- by installments. Even after acceptance of such payment the respondent filed Certificate Case No. 127/90 for recovery of Tk. 2.619 Million in local currency Tk. 0.5000 million with interest. The petitioner instituted of Title Suit No. 44/90 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Moulvibazar for declaration that Certificate case filed malafide and it was void. The suit was contested by the respondent. During the trial one Mr. Khalid Hossain, Principal Officer of Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Shansta deposed admitting that Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangsta imported machineries and the petitioner has, no choice to purchase the machinery and the loan was paid in yen as noted above. The learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit with the finding that the claim for recovery of the loan amount "is in serious dispute". In the meantime after the decree was made respondent instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 260/92 in 2 Artha Rin Adalat, Dhaka under section 33 of the Bangladesh Shilpa Sangstha Order, 1972 (P.O. 128/72) claiming for a decree of Tk. 3,114/- Million with interest thereon. The petitioner, on the other hand, instituted Title Suit No. 5/94 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Moulvibazar claiming damage of Tk. 1,00,00,000/- During pendency of the suits the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha, the respondent, advertised for sale of the property for recovery of the loan amount. The dispute raised ultimately went before the Appellate Division on the question of injunction. Appellate Division by its order dated 4.6.97 granted leave stayed the operation of the injunction holding that High Court Division failed to consider the bar provided in Article 34 of the aforesaid Order in granting injunction. It further held that Article 34 is a provision of special law and shall prevail over general law. And held that the trial court in granting temporary injunction acted contrary to the scheme of the legislation which is a special one meaning the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangsta Order, 1972. 

 2. The questions that fall our determination for disposal of this application are whether, as contended by Mr. Sinha, in a case of disputed demand can there be application of section 34 of the Order for sale of the property to recover the amount under demand. Secondly, whether prior to taking possession of the mill itself by the respondent such advertisement for direct sale under section 34 can be made. Thirdly, whether the officer of the respondent having had deposed before the Civil Court and such deposition giving rise to a dispute regarding the amount to be recovered by instituting a civil suit issuance of notice under section 34 of the Order can be maintained in law. Mr. Sinha in continuation of his contention has taken us through the provision of section 34 of the Order and also cited a decision in the case of New Ideal Engineering Works Vs. Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangsta, 42 DLR 221(AD).
